result:
That's not quite right — more agents doesn't always mean better results. Splitting work across agents adds real costs: every extra agent is another model call, which means more latency, more tokens burned, and more places for a handoff to go wrong (one agent misreading what another meant). With a small sponsor budget, that overhead matters a lot.

Think of it like staffing a small kitchen for one dish. One cook who knows the recipe and has the right tools (knife, pan, oven) just cooks it. If you put ten cooks in that kitchen, they're not ten times faster — they're bumping into each other, waiting for the stove, and someone has to coordinate who does what. More hands only help when the dish actually has independent parts happening at once, like one person on the sauce while another handles the dough.

Same with your makerspace assistant. Answering a manual question, checking the calendar, and booking a slot are mostly a straight line — one step depends on the last. One agent with three good tools (manual search, calendar check, booking) can walk that line itself, calling each tool when it needs it. Splitting that into five or ten agents just adds coordination and cost for no real gain, because there's nothing happening in parallel and no step that needs a genuinely different kind of specialist.

Multiple agents pay off when pieces are truly independent or need different expertise — not just because more sounds more thorough.

Does the kitchen picture make sense for why more cooks isn't automatically faster here?
